endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: For the avoidance of doubt, a change shall constitute a Material Modification regardless of whether it is accompanied by a version number or product name update.

endorsements.title: Equity at the point of care: auditing AI-supported resource allocation in obstetric emergencies
endorsements.quote: Any change to trigger logic, thresholds, routing, interfaces, or data-field mappings requires versioned change control and re-audit of chain metrics and stratified gaps.

endorsements.title: Governing Patient-Facing AI-Generated Video in Digital Health: A Risk-and-Ethics Matrix for Deployment, Monitoring, and Change Control
endorsements.quote: Approvals in “permit with oversight” should be time limited and coupled with predefined rereview triggers (eg, model or prompt updates, distribution channel changes, sentinel incidents, or emerging inequities).

endorsements.title: Risk Management of Large Language Model-Based Exercise and Health Guidance: A China-Anchored, Comparatively Informed Six-Dimensional Trigger Matrix and Lifecycle Governance Framework for the Wellness-to-SaMD Continuum
endorsements.quote: These transitions should be assessed before deployment and after every material change to claims, data, automation, or model configuration.

commentary.bottom_line: Four sources, one framework and three commentaries, endorse defining reassessment triggers for material changes to AI tools, including changes made without a new version number, but no supplied study tests the practice or documents the hazard. The recommendation currently rests on expert consensus rather than measured outcomes.

perspectives.view: No study in the supplied set tests whether reassessment triggers change outcomes, and no study measures how often materially changed AI stays in use without review. The four endorsements are a framework and three commentaries. Under GRADE conventions, expert opinion without tested comparisons does not yield a certainty rating above no direct evidence.

The CHAI playbook states that a change counts as a material modification whether or not a version number or product name changes. This language sets a governance expectation, but the supplied sources report no evaluation of whether health systems that adopt such definitions detect more unannounced changes than those that do not.

The endorsing commentaries list threshold edits, routing, data-field mappings, prompt updates, and sentinel incidents as candidate triggers. No supplied study reports how often these changes occur or whether they cause harm, so the size of the hazard and the share of errors a trigger policy would catch remain unmeasured.

commentary.research_gap: No study compares organizations or tools with and without defined reassessment triggers, and none measures the frequency of silent vendor or local configuration changes, the delay before they are detected, or the performance and equity shifts that follow. Prospective audits that log changes against trigger definitions and track downstream error and subgroup performance would supply the first direct evidence.
commentary.underserved_note: No supplied study tested the practice in any population, so no evidence exists for Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients. One commentary on obstetric resource allocation calls for re-auditing stratified gaps after changes, which suggests equity monitoring could be tied to triggers, but that link has not been evaluated.
